paras: The killing of Ernest Green was the fatal shooting of a Black boy, 13 or 14 years old, by Elizabeth M. Flagler, daughter of the army's chief of ordnance, who fired from an upstairs window at boys taking pears outside her family's home in Washington, D.C., on August 2, 1895. A coroner's jury found that same evening that she had fired "carelessly and indifferently" but could not be held, a verdict that drew protest from Black Washingtonians and comment across the country. She later gave $10,000 bail to await a grand jury, which had not taken up the case by the end of September.

Families near the Flagler house on California avenue had complained for weeks of boys, "both white and colored," who took fruit and broke branches. Flagler, alone at home, said she had fired into the road the previous Monday and warned the boys she would shoot at them if they returned, meaning, she said, only to scare them.

On the morning of August 2 about eight Black boys passed the house on the way to a ball game, and Green, by most accounts, put his hand through the iron fence for pears. Hearing the branches rustle, Flagler took a pistol from her bureau and fired twice from the window; she said she fired in haste and, being near-sighted, did not see the boy fall. Green ran a short way, fell several times, and died in the Flagler house before the police surgeon arrived. Flagler then surrendered at police headquarters.

At the inquest that afternoon lawyers and Green's pastor, Rev. J. A. Taylor, attended for the family, and R. Ross Perry for Flagler, whose voluntary statement the jurors were not allowed to question. After the jury declared it could not hold her, she was released and taken out a back way past a crowd of several hundred. Juror George M. J. Dorsey later told the Evening Star that the clause clearing her had been written in at Perry's suggestion after the jurors signed. The prosecutor treated the verdict as a finding of manslaughter, and on August 7 Judge Cole admitted Flagler to bail.

About 2,500 people attended the funeral on August 4, where Taylor said Green "had been killed because human life in this city amounts to nothing" and Rev. Walter H. Brooks said that "to take human life without just cause is no crime in Washington." Col. Perry Carson called an indignation meeting, but Black lawyers including W. Calvin Chase, editor of the Bee, urged waiting for the grand jury. When the meeting opened on August 7, Taylor conveyed the parents' wish that nothing be done, and it adjourned.
On September 12 District Attorney Birney said he would present the case to the October grand jury; no report of grand jury action appears in the coverage through September.

The Evening Star and the Morning Times printed the inquest testimony nearly word for word. Early headlines put the theft first: the Star's read "HE WAS ATTEMPTING TO STEAL FRUIT," and wire versions called Green "a Little Negro Boy Who Was Stealing Fruit," a "Young Trespasser" and "the Boy Apple Thief."

Within days the New York Sun reported Black residents' argument that the verdict would have differed had "a colored girl killed a white boy," and editorials in the Indianapolis Journal and the Pawtucket Tribune called the act manslaughter or said pears were not worth a life. A Washington special in the Rock Island Argus instead predicted no indictment and praised the father for refusing "colored lawyers."

The one Black-press report in the coverage, a brief in the Topeka Weekly Call on August 17, called Green "a promising thirteen year old boy" who reached through the fence "childlike," named Flagler as "a white girl," and said the jury had acquitted her.

The first wire report said Flagler warned the boys and that the ball entered Green's head, killing him instantly. At the inquest, however, the autopsy placed the entry wound in his back, witnesses said he lived for some minutes, and her coachman heard no warning. The boys said no white boys were with them at the tree, while Flagler's servant thought most were white.

reader.title: Killing of Ernest Green
bases: A single white woman, Elizabeth M. Flagler, shot a Black boy from her window over fruit taken from her father's tree; no mob, band, posse or officers were involved (A2, A6, A33).

The local Evening Star and Morning Times, wire reports and the Black-press Weekly Call agree that Flagler shot and killed Green on August 2 and that a coroner's jury did not hold her (A2, A5, A6, A3, A33).

accounts.label: First wire report
accounts.gist: Flagler warned the boys from the window, then fired an army revolver at Green in the yard, the ball entering his head and killing him instantly.

accounts.label: Evening Star local report and autopsy
accounts.gist: Green was at the fence reaching for pears when a .32 bullet passed through his chest; the autopsy found it entered his back, and he died in the Flagler house.

accounts.label: The boys' testimony
accounts.gist: About eight Black boys bound for a ball game stopped (or Green alone stopped) at the fence; Green reached through for pears; the first shot hit him and the second passed Lynch's head.

accounts.label: Flagler's statement
accounts.gist: Near-sighted, she fired hurriedly toward the road to frighten boys who had been stealing fruit, meaning to fire low as she had on Monday, and did not see the boy fall.

accounts.label: Juror Dorsey
accounts.gist: The jury's signed verdict ended with the finding of carelessness; the clause 'we cannot hold' was written in afterward at Perry's suggestion, and he had meant the case to go to the grand jury.

accounts.label: Black correspondent (Weekly Call)
accounts.gist: A promising 13-year-old reached through the fence for fruit on the ground; Flagler, 'a white girl', fired twice from upstairs, and the inquest acquitted her.

framing.detail: The Evening Star's first headlines ('HE WAS ATTEMPTING TO STEAL FRUIT') and its admiring portrait of Flagler gave way to detailed testimony, the juror's charge and Black criticism.
Wire versions led with the theft ('Killed a Little Negro Boy Who Was Stealing Fruit', 'Negroes Excited', 'the Boy Apple Thief', 'Young Trespasser').
Editorial paragraphs in the Indianapolis Journal and Pawtucket Tribune said pears were not worth a life and that the act was manslaughter.
The New York Sun reported Black indignation and the argument that the verdict would differ if a Black girl had killed a white boy, while noting 'the best people' sympathized with Flagler.
A Washington special in the Rock Island Argus predicted no indictment, praised the father's restraint and said he had spurned colored lawyers seeking notoriety.
The Weekly Call called Green 'a promising thirteen year old boy' acting 'childlike', named the shooter as 'a white girl', and said the jury 'acquitted' her.
